html:
Mansa Musa was the ninth mansa, or king, of the Mali Empire, ruling from about 1312 to about 1337, when Mali reached its greatest size. He is remembered above all for his wealth.

By the account he gave in Cairo, his predecessor sailed into the Atlantic with a great fleet and never came back, and Musa took the throne.

In 1324 he made the pilgrimage to Mecca with a huge caravan and a great deal of gold. He spent and gave away so much in Cairo that the price of gold there fell. Word of him spread to Europe: the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows a crowned African king on a throne holding a gold nugget.

During his reign Mali took Gao and Timbuktu. He came home with Muslim scholars and the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq es-Sahili, and is linked to the Djinguereber mosque in Timbuktu. Islamic learning in the Sahel grew under his patronage, carried by the trans-Saharan trade.

He is often called the richest person who ever lived, but no real figure can be put on his wealth; contemporaries simply described it as beyond counting. In Mandinka oral tradition he matters less than the founder, Sundiata Keita.
